Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e111.summary: Rubric giving the title of Prologue Question 3: on the formal, efficient, and final causes of theology.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e118.summary: Divisio paragraph: having treated the material cause of sacred doctrine, Giles turns to the remaining causes — the final cause (whether theology's end is praxis or speculation), the efficient cause (whether God alone teaches it), and the formal cause, which yields two questions because form gives being (is Scripture wisdom or science?) and the mode of acting, which reduces to form, grounds a science's certitude (is it more or less certain than other sciences?).
claims: The formal cause of a science bears both on what it is and on its mode of proceeding, which determines its certitude.
The remaining causes of theology raise four questions: wisdom vs. science, certitude, who teaches it, and practical vs. speculative.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e165.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 1: whether Sacred Scripture is wisdom.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e172.summary: First argument that Scripture is not wisdom: it belongs to the wise to order (Metaph. 1), and a science orders another by giving it regulating principles, which theology does not do for any science.
claims: Ordering other sciences means providing their principles, which theology does not do.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e190.summary: Second argument: order consists in reducing many to one, and in every genus there is one thing to which all are reduced (Pseudo-Dionysius); the one science to which the sciences are reduced deserves the name wisdom; that is metaphysics (Metaph. 1); so theology is not wisdom.
claims: Only one science can be the wisdom to which all sciences are reduced, and that is metaphysics.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e224.summary: Sed contra: the wise in each genus is the one who considers the highest in that genus; since science is always of being, and theology considers the highest being, it is most of all wisdom among sciences. Then a second question is opened: theology seems not to be science, since Augustine (De Trinitate 14) distinguishes wisdom from science.
claims: Theology is wisdom because it considers the highest in the genus of beings.
If wisdom is distinguished from science, theology as wisdom would not be science.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e253.summary: Further argument that theology is not science: demonstration is a syllogism that makes one know, and knowing is through demonstration (Post. An. 1); theology does not demonstrate; so it does not deserve the name of science.
claims: Scientific knowledge is by demonstration, which theology lacks.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e269.summary: Sed contra (on science): Augustine (De Trinitate 14) attributes 'science' not to whatever humans can know but only to that concerning faith, thereby calling theology a science.
claims: Augustine calls knowledge concerning faith 'science'.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e282.summary: Second sed contra: Augustine says the Apostle properly calls 'science' the knowledge of how faith may help the pious and be defended against the impious; since theology does this, it is properly called science.
claims: Theology, as nourishing and defending faith, is properly science in Augustine's sense.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e302.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is properly wisdom.
claims: Theology is properly wisdom.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e310.summary: Preliminary to the determinatio: whether it befits us to dispute about wisdom at all, since, following Augustine (De Trinitate 14), if only the wise may dispute about wisdom, and we should not profess ourselves wise (as Pythagoras called himself a lover of wisdom rather than wise), the question would be idle; but Augustine allows that lovers of wisdom may also dispute about it.
claims: Lovers of wisdom, not only the wise, may legitimately dispute about wisdom.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e377.summary: Determinatio, first distinction: taken broadly, wisdom and science can each be called by the other's name (Augustine, De Trinitate 13), but properly, science is knowledge of human things and wisdom of divine things. In the proper sense theology alone is wisdom, since other sciences treat divine things in a human mode, or not at all, or not as their first and principal object in every way, whereas theology treats God in a divine mode, by revelation, and principally in every way. Giles adds confirmation from the six conditions of the wise in Metaph. 1 — knowing all things, knowing difficult things, knowing with certainty, considering causes of causes, being for its own sake, and ordering rather than being ordered — and shows the first applies to theology because it knows things distinctly, not only universally.
claims: Properly, science is knowledge of human things and wisdom of divine things.
Theology alone is properly wisdom because it treats God in the divine mode, principally and in every way.
The six Aristotelian marks of the wise apply most of all to the theologian.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e513.summary: Applies the remaining Aristotelian conditions of wisdom to theology: it knows all things, using all sciences in its service; it treats the most difficult, since God, most manifest in nature, is to our eye as light to the owl; it is most certain (to be shown in Art. 2); it considers causes of causes, since the first truth causes all truths as fire all hot things (Metaph. 2); it alone among wayfarers' sciences is for its own sake and free; and it orders all others as military art orders bridle-making. Hence the name of wisdom belongs to it (Ecclesiasticus 6).
claims: Theology satisfies all six Aristotelian conditions of wisdom.
God, though most manifest in nature, is most difficult for us to know.
Theology alone among wayfarers' sciences is free and for its own sake.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e600.summary: Second distinction, on the side of what theology considers: things considered principally, the divine, by reason of which it is called wisdom, and things considered consequently, the human, by reason of which it can be called science. So theology is science only on the broad usage, and properly wisdom; or, by the second distinction, wisdom regarding its principal objects and science regarding its secondary ones.
claims: Theology is wisdom with respect to what it principally considers (divine things) and science with respect to what it considers consequently (human things).
Properly speaking, theology is called only wisdom.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e646.summary: Replies to the arguments against wisdom: (1) the wise need not give principles to other sciences, only use them in its service, as shown in the question on order; (2) metaphysics is the one wise science among human sciences but not wise simpliciter, the theologian being wiser by searching God more deeply; it is no difficulty for a multitude to be reduced to several 'ones' if one of them is ordered to another, as human sciences are ordered to metaphysics and metaphysics to theology.
claims: Wisdom orders by using other sciences in its service, not by giving them principles.
Metaphysics is wisdom only within human sciences; theology is wiser simpliciter.
Human sciences are ordered to metaphysics, and metaphysics to theology.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e686.summary: Reply to the argument that theology is not science: it is not science in the proper sense, but in the common sense, or with respect to what it considers consequently rather than principally; this also explains Augustine's apparent assertion that theology is properly science.
claims: Theology is science only in the broad sense or with respect to its secondary objects.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e711.summary: Reply to the demonstration argument: theology demonstrates not as geometry but as perspective does, presupposing the articles of faith; since arts proceeding this way are sciences, theology should be called a science.
claims: Theology demonstrates as a subalternated science, presupposing the articles of faith as principles.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e736.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 2: whether theology is more certain than other sciences.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e743.summary: Arguments against theology's greater certitude: (1) mathematical demonstrations are in the first order of certitude (Averroes, Metaph. 2); (2) theology and metaphysics are both wisdom, so they must differ in mode of proceeding, and metaphysics proceeds most certainly (Metaph. 1), so theology does not.
claims: Mathematical demonstrations hold the first rank of certitude.
Since metaphysics proceeds most certainly, theology, differing from it in mode, must be less certain.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e776.summary: Third argument: the more clearly we see things the more certain we are; other sciences, proceeding by reason from sense, give clearer sight of their objects; so they are more certain.
claims: Sciences rooted in sense and reason give clearer, hence more certain, knowledge.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e790.summary: Sed contra: Christ shows us infallible truth about eternal things (Augustine, De Trinitate 13); something is certain insofar as it is true and infallible; theology has such truth; so it is more certain.
claims: Certitude follows infallible truth, which theology receives from Christ.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e811.summary: Second sed contra: what is more subject to error is less certain (the principle of non-contradiction is firmest because least erred about, Metaph. 4); philosophers erred in their sciences but theologians did not (Hugh of St. Victor); so theology is more certain.
claims: Freedom from error indicates greater certitude, and theologians, unlike philosophers, have not erred.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e833.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is more certain than other sciences, though not by way of clear speculation.
claims: Theology is more certain than other sciences, but not in the certitude of clear speculation.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e842.summary: Determinatio distinguishes three sources of certitude — the things considered, the light relied upon, and the science's proportion to the knowers — and analyzes the first into three members: a science is more certain if its objects are prior rather than by addition (arithmetic over geometry, the point being 'unity with position'), if they are less sensible (mathematics over physics), and if it gives propter quid rather than quia (geometry over perspective), the latter two being virtually contained in the first. Since theology is about God, principle of all principles (Pseudo-Dionysius), and is not principally about sensibles at all, every mode of certitude based on the science in itself belongs to it.
claims: Certitude in a science derives from its objects, its light, or its proportion to knowers.
With respect to objects, sciences of principles, of less sensible things, and of the propter quid are more certain, the latter two reducing to the first.
Theology possesses every mode of certitude based on the science in itself, since it is about the first principle and not about sensibles.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e975.summary: Second source of certitude, the light: one relying on supernatural light can claim more infallible truth than one relying on reason about the same things; Aristotle did not treat this because he thought we know only by the agent intellect's light; in this respect too theology is most certain, and nothing is held more certainly than what is grasped by faith.
claims: Knowledge resting on supernatural light is more certain than knowledge resting on natural reason.
Aristotle ignored this source of certitude because he recognized only the agent intellect's light.
Nothing is held more certainly than what faith apprehends.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1010.summary: Third source of certitude, relative to knowers, is twofold: certitude of adhesion, in which theology is most certain since no one would undergo capital punishment for any other science's truth; and certitude of speculation, in which theology is not most certain, because it concerns objects of faith, which is of things not seen.
claims: Theology has the greatest certitude of adhesion, as shown by martyrdom.
Theology lacks the greatest certitude of speculation because faith concerns things not seen.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1044.summary: Replies: (1) mathematical demonstrations are first in certitude relative to natural ones, or among human sciences, since Averroes recognized no science in man but humanly invented ones; (2) metaphysics differs from theology in certitude by being, simply speaking, less certain (sentence continues).
claims: Mathematics is first in certitude only relative to natural or human sciences.
Metaphysics is simpliciter less certain than theology.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1075.summary: Completes the replies: Aristotle's calling metaphysics most certain applies within human sciences; theology's other differences from metaphysics are left aside; (3) the argument rightly concludes that other sciences are more certain by way of speculation, but theology excels in other modes of certitude, so it is more certain simpliciter.
claims: Metaphysics is most certain only within the genus of human sciences.
Other sciences are more certain in speculation, but theology is more certain simpliciter.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1114.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 3: whether God alone teaches this science.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1121.summary: Arguments that God alone teaches theology (its efficient cause): (1) no one teaches what he does not possess, and divine science is not a human possession — only God has it (Metaph. 1, Simonides); (2) knowledge requires the presence of a species in the intellect (De anima 3), which an angel cannot create since nature obeys it only as to motion, not form, and still less can a human.
claims: Divine science is not a human possession, so humans cannot teach it.
Neither angels nor humans can create intelligible species in another's intellect.
concepts: divine science as possession of God

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1169.summary: Third argument: Augustine (De disciplina christiana) says he who has his chair in heaven teaches hearts on earth, and the Head teaches its members; so a mere human cannot teach this science.
claims: Christ, teaching from heaven, is the true teacher of hearts.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1193.summary: Sed contra: teaching is making another know; if God can teach us and we can know, then since the ability to teach is the sign of a knower (Metaph. 1), humans can teach this science; moreover, angels taught the holy fathers many things (Pseudo-Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy).
claims: The ability to teach is a sign of knowledge, so those who know theology can teach it.
Angels taught the patriarchs, so God is not the only teacher.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1219.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: God teaches in every way; humans and angels in some way.
claims: God teaches in every way; angels and humans teach only in some way.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1228.summary: Reports an opinion ('secundum quosdam') distinguishing three agents — universal, particular, and administrative — as in nature (the celestial body or God; the nature of the grain; the physician who applies what helps nature), and applying it to teaching: God is the universal agent, human reason the particular, and human or angel the administrative; just as nature has seminal beginnings, the intellect has 'seeds' of the sciences, first principles naturally implanted by God, from which science arises.
claims: (Reported) In teaching, God is the universal agent, human reason the particular agent, and humans or angels administrative agents.
(Reported) First principles are seeds of science naturally implanted by God in each intellect.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1298.summary: Criticizes the reported opinion: though it would solve the question, its fabric is weak because it assumes falsely that principles are innate; the intellect begins as a blank tablet, and principles are acquired through sense, memory, and experience, since it would be absurd to possess the noblest habits without knowing it (Post. An. 2); how principles are 'naturally known' is deferred to Book 2.
claims: The intellect is originally a tabula rasa.
First principles are acquired through sense, memory, and experience, not innate.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1335.summary: Giles's own answer: knowledge requires light and an ordering of species, as vision requires light and the direct, ordered multiplication of species to the eye; since mind is to soul as eye to body (Damascene), understanding requires the light of the agent intellect actualizing the possible intellect, and the right ordering of species, as letters rightly ordered make syllables and words. One can teach another regarding light by creating it or strengthening it, and regarding order of species. An angel creates no light, neither natural (agent intellect) nor gratuitous (faith, grace), but can strengthen our light, as a burning coal is intensified by another, and can order our phantasms toward the sensitive principle; whether it can directly cause species in the intellect is deferred to Book 2.
claims: Knowing requires both intellectual light and a right ordering of species, as seeing does.
Teaching may act on the learner's light (creating or strengthening it) or on the order of species.
Angels cannot create natural or gratuitous light in us but can strengthen it and order our phantasms.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1457.summary: Concludes: humans can do less than angels, neither creating light nor uniting themselves to it to strengthen it, but can in some way order phantasms by speaking or writing things in order, moving the hearer or reader to knowledge. Thus God teaches in every way (creating and strengthening light and ordering species), angels in some way (strengthening light and ordering phantasms), humans least (only ordering phantasms); and since angels and humans teach by divine power, it is sometimes granted that God alone teaches.
claims: Human teachers can only order the learner's phantasms through ordered speech or writing.
God teaches in every way, angels in some ways, humans in the fewest.
Because creatures teach by divine power, it can be said that God alone teaches.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1504.summary: Replies: (1) God alone has divine science maximally, not that humans have it in no way; so God alone teaches it maximally, and it is not called a human possession because humans do not have it perfectly in this life; (2) the angel need not cause species for a person to learn; it suffices to bring forth in order phantasms hidden in memory or latent in species; (3) Augustine means not that humans in no way teach but that they do not teach principally.
claims: Humans possess divine science imperfectly in this life, God maximally.
Angels teach by ordering latent phantasms, not by creating species.
Humans teach, but not principally.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1553.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 4: whether theology is a practical or speculative science.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1562.summary: Introduces the final cause question (sciences have praxis or speculation as end) and gives the first argument that theology is practical: the end of moral science is action, not knowing (Ethics 1); theology teaches most about morals; so its end is action and it is practical.
claims: Since theology teaches morals and moral science aims at action, theology seems practical.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1595.summary: Second argument: life is the formal element in each thing, and faith receives life from good works ('faith without works is dead', James); since theology and faith concern the same things, Scripture receives its perfection from good works, and a thing is ordered to its perfection as to its end; so theology's end is operation.
claims: Faith is perfected by works, and theology shares faith's objects, so its end is operation.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1618.summary: Third argument: sciences that exist so that we may become good are practical; theology is such most of all.
claims: Theology aims to make us good, which marks a practical science.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1627.summary: Opening of the sed contra: the science of what is most speculable is most speculative (sentence continues).

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1634.summary: Completes the sed contra: God is most intelligible and speculable, so the science of God is most speculative; and the whole reward is promised in vision (Augustine, De Trinitate 1), which belongs to speculation.
claims: The science of God, the most speculable object, is most speculative.
The whole reward consists in vision, which is speculative.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1652.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is more speculative than practical, and can be called affective.
claims: Theology is more speculative than practical and is properly called affective.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1661.summary: Determinatio begins with a principle on plural ends: a thing may have several ends if one is ordered to another (as war to victory); then the ultimate end is that in whose power the others move and which is intended in all of them, while it is not intended in them — as the first agent's power extends to every effect of secondary agents but not vice versa.
claims: A thing can have several ends if they are ordered to one another.
The ultimate end is intended in all the subordinate ends, as the first agent's power is present in all secondary agency.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1716.summary: Applies the principle: other ends are intended only in some way; Scripture intends several ends, and first good operation, since it treats morals most and the end of moral teaching is action.
claims: Scripture intends several ends, among them good operation.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1741.summary: Continues: Scripture also intends speculation, since it treats the most speculable things, and love, since the end of the commandment is charity; one of these must be principal, namely the one intended everywhere; since love and charity are intended throughout Scripture, on which the Law and Prophets depend, the principal end of Scripture is to lead humans to the love of God and neighbor.
claims: Scripture intends operation, speculation, and love.
The principal end of Scripture is to lead humans to love of God and neighbor, since charity is intended throughout it.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1774.summary: Confirms with Augustine that charity is intended universally in Scripture ('hold charity, on which all depends... charity is manifest in what you understand, hidden in what you do not'); since a thing is named from its principal end (De anima 2), theology should be named from charity; and since charity is in the affect, not the intellect (which alone divides into speculative and practical), theology is properly neither speculative nor practical but affective — wisdom more because it leads to savoring (sapor) divine things than because it makes one know them. If forced to choose, it is more speculative than practical, since divine vision bears more principally on beatitude than operation does. Replies begin: (1) action is in some way, not simply, its end; (2) faith's perfection by works is not simpliciter, since works have their goodness from charity (1 Corinthians 13; sentence continues).
claims: Charity is the principal end of Scripture, intended throughout it.
Because charity resides in the affect, theology is properly an affective science, neither speculative nor practical.
Theology is wisdom chiefly as leading to the savor of divine things.
Compared with practical, theology is more speculative, since vision bears more on beatitude than operation.
Works have their goodness from charity.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1886.summary: Completes the second reply: 'if I deliver my body to be burned but have not charity, it profits me nothing'; hence charity, not works, is called the form of the virtues.
claims: Charity, not works, is the form of the virtues.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1895.summary: Remaining replies: (3) theology exists that we may become good, but our goodness here comes by infusion, not from works; Aristotle's principle that we become good by doing good (Ethics 2) does not hold theologically, where we do good because we are good. (Sed contra 1) theology is speculative compared to praxis, but more affective; as it concerns the most speculable it also concerns the most lovable, and in this life it attains love more than knowledge (Hugh of St. Victor: love enters where knowledge stays outside). (Sed contra 2) vision is the whole reward not simpliciter but as it extends to the affect (continued).
claims: Theological goodness is infused, not acquired by repeated acts; we do good because we are good.
In this life theology attains love more than knowledge.
Love surpasses knowledge, entering where knowledge remains outside.
Vision is the complete reward only as it extends to the affect.

Gi9qrR-de6352-d1e1950.summary: Sentence fragment completing the last reply: vision is the whole reward insofar as it extends to the affect, as will be shown in its proper place.

Gi9qrR-de6352-Dd1e157.summary: Article 1 asks whether Scripture is wisdom and whether it is science. After justifying a lover of wisdom's right to dispute about wisdom (Augustine on Pythagoras), Giles distinguishes broad from proper usage: properly, science concerns human and wisdom divine things, so theology alone, treating God in the divine mode by revelation and principally in every way, is properly wisdom, satisfying all six Aristotelian marks of the wise (knowing all, difficult, certain, causes of causes, for its own sake, ordering others). A second distinction lets theology be called wisdom regarding its principal (divine) objects and science regarding its consequent (human) ones. The replies explain that wisdom orders by using other sciences rather than giving their principles, that metaphysics is wise only among human sciences and is itself ordered to theology, and that theology demonstrates like perspective, from presupposed articles of faith.
claims: Theology is properly wisdom, not science.
Theology can be called science broadly or with respect to its secondary objects.
Theology fulfills the six Aristotelian conditions of wisdom more than metaphysics.
Theology demonstrates as a subalternated science from the articles of faith.

Gi9qrR-de6352-Dd1e728.summary: Article 2 determines that theology is more certain than other sciences simpliciter, though not in clarity of speculation. Giles distinguishes three sources of certitude: from the objects (priority of principles, less sensibility, propter quid — all of which theology possesses maximally as being about God, principle of principles); from the light (theology rests on supernatural light, a source Aristotle ignored, so nothing is held more certainly than what faith grasps); and from relation to knowers, divided into certitude of adhesion (greatest in theology, as martyrdom shows) and of speculation (lesser, since faith is of things unseen). The replies restrict the primacy of mathematics and metaphysics in certitude to human sciences.
claims: Theology is simpliciter more certain than all other sciences.
Certitude derives from objects, light, and proportion to knowers.
Theology excels in certitude of object, light, and adhesion, but not of speculation.
Mathematics and metaphysics are most certain only among human sciences.

Gi9qrR-de6352-Dd1e1106.summary: Article 3, on theology's efficient cause, holds that God teaches it in every way and angels and humans only in some way. Giles rejects a reported account (God as universal, reason as particular, and humans/angels as administrative agents, working on innate 'seeds' of science) because it presupposes innate principles, whereas the intellect is a blank tablet and principles are acquired through sense, memory, and experience. His own account models knowing on seeing: it requires intellectual light and the ordering of species. God can create and strengthen light and order species; angels cannot create natural or gratuitous light but can strengthen ours and order our phantasms; humans can only order phantasms through ordered speech and writing. Since creatures teach by divine power, it may be said that God alone teaches.
claims: God teaches in every way; angels and humans teach in limited ways.
First principles are acquired, not innate; the intellect begins as a tabula rasa.
Knowing requires intellectual light and the ordering of species.
Human teaching consists in ordering the learner's phantasms.

Gi9qrR-de6352-Dd1e1545.summary: Article 4, on theology's final cause, argues that Scripture intends several ordered ends — good operation, speculation, and love — of which the principal, intended throughout (as Augustine's praise of charity shows), is leading humans to love of God and neighbor. Since a thing is named from its principal end and charity resides in the affect rather than the intellect (which alone divides into speculative and practical), theology is properly an affective science, wisdom chiefly as savor of divine things; compared with practical, however, it is more speculative, because vision bears more on beatitude than operation. The replies stress that works derive their goodness from charity, the form of the virtues; that theological goodness is infused, so we do good because we are good; and that in this life theology attains love more than knowledge.
claims: The principal end of Scripture is charity, the love of God and neighbor.
Theology is properly an affective science, neither speculative nor practical.
Compared with practical, theology is more speculative.
Theological goodness is infused, not acquired through works.

Gi9qrR-de6352.summary: Prologue, Question 3 completes Giles's four-cause analysis of theology with its formal, efficient, and final causes. On the formal cause, theology is properly wisdom rather than science, satisfying all of Aristotle's marks of the wise because it treats God principally in the divine mode, and being science only broadly or regarding its secondary objects (Art. 1); and it is simpliciter more certain than all other sciences in its object, its supernatural light, and the adhesion it commands, though less certain in clarity of speculation, since faith is of things unseen (Art. 2). On the efficient cause, God alone teaches it in every way — creating and strengthening light and ordering species — while angels and humans teach in limited, instrumental ways, humans only by ordering phantasms, and principles are acquired from sense rather than innate (Art. 3). On the final cause, its principal end is charity, so it is properly an affective science, though more speculative than practical (Art. 4).
claims: Theology is properly wisdom rather than science.
Theology is simpliciter the most certain science, though not in clarity of speculation.
God teaches theology in every way; angels and humans only instrumentally and partially.
Theology's principal end is charity, making it properly an affective science, more speculative than practical.
